title: Gallstone treatment: comparing observation and procedures
intro: Treatment depends on whether stones cause symptoms, where they are and whether complications are present. Removing the gallbladder is different from clearing a bile duct. A scan finding alone does not automatically mean surgery is needed.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Observation is usual for many symptom-free gallbladder stones, with selected exceptions. For recurrent typical attacks, discuss likely benefit and whether other digestive symptoms may have another cause and persist after surgery.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: Ultrasound, blood tests and selected duct imaging guide decisions. Ask if a stone blocks drainage, whether infection or pancreatitis is suspected and how urgent treatment is. Your overall health affects procedural planning. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Gallbladder removal is often laparoscopic but still has anesthetic, bleeding, infection and bile-duct injury risks. Duct stones may require endoscopic removal, which has its own risks including pancreatitis; it does not automatically remove the gallbladder stones. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Medicines may relieve pain; stone-dissolving treatment suits only selected cases and stones can recur. Commercial flushes are not reliable cures. Ask about recovery, work, driving and support at home before a planned procedure. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Fever, jaundice, severe persistent pain or repeated vomiting requires urgent assessment, even if surgery is scheduled. After a procedure, follow instructions for worsening pain, fever, jaundice or wound problems rather than assuming all symptoms are normal recovery.
